h1: Using Indian six-row barley for malt whisky: what distillers face
title: Indian Six-Row Barley for Malt Whisky | Craft Beer School
desc: What distillers face when making malt whisky from Indian six-row barley: protein, husk, enzymes, milling, yield and how to adjust mashing and fermentation.
teaser: More husk, more protein, smaller grains. Indian six-row barley can make fine malt whisky if you plan for it.
standfirst: Most of the textbooks on malt whisky assume plump two-row barley from cool climates. Indian distillers often work with six-row barley grown in hot, dry states. It behaves differently at every step from the mill to the still.
sections: Two-row and six-row: the basic difference

Barley ears carry their kernels in either two rows or six. In two-row barley the kernels are larger and more even. In six-row barley the side kernels are smaller and often twisted, so a sample has a wider spread of sizes.

Six-row barley usually carries more husk and more protein, which means less starch per kilogram. It also tends to have higher enzyme power, because more protein goes with more enzymes after malting. India grows mostly six-row barley, much of it in Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. Our guide to the barley malting process explains how that grain becomes malt.
What it means for spirit yield

Lower starch means less fermentable extract per tonne. Less extract means fewer litres of alcohol per tonne of malt. Distillers usually track spirit yield in litres of pure alcohol per tonne. Expect six-row malt to sit below the figures quoted for premium two-row distilling malt. Set your budget and pricing on your own measured yield rather than a European benchmark.

Always ask the maltster for a certificate of analysis on each lot: moisture, extract, total protein, friability and diastatic power at minimum. Our guide to reading a malt certificate of analysis explains each number. Lot-to-lot variation is often larger in local barley, so test before you commit a full silo.

Mixed kernel sizes are hard to mill evenly. A roller gap set for the plump kernels lets the small ones through whole. That starch never reaches the mash. Set the gap for the small kernels and the big ones shatter into flour, which can set the mash and slow run-off.

Screening the malt and checking a grist sample with a sieve set is cheap insurance. Many distillers find a two-pass or multi-roller mill handles six-row better than a single pair of rolls. The extra husk is one blessing here: it gives a looser filter bed in the mash tun or lauter tun.

High diastatic power is useful. It converts starch quickly and can carry a share of unmalted grain if your recipe or rules allow. The catch is the protein. More protein brings more free amino nitrogen, which feeds yeast well, but also more haze-forming material and potential for foaming in the washback.

Most malt distilleries mash at around 63 to 65 °C to favour fermentable sugars, since the wash is not boiled and every sugar the yeast can use becomes alcohol. Watch the first wort gravity and the final grains. Starch left in the spent grain is lost yield. A simple iodine test on the run-off tells you whether conversion finished.

The richer nitrogen in six-row wort often means a vigorous, fast fermentation. In Indian heat that can push washback temperatures well above the low 30s °C unless you have cooling, which stresses the yeast and raises fusel alcohols. Pitch at a moderate temperature, control the peak and allow time for the slower, fruitier phase late in fermentation.

Six-row barley gives a slightly more grainy, husky character to new make than plump two-row malt. That is not a flaw. Some Indian distillers treat it as part of their house style rather than something to hide.
Storing malt in Indian heat and humidity

Malt leaves the maltster at low moisture, typically around 4 to 5%. In a humid Indian monsoon it pulls water from the air quickly. Slack malt mills poorly, crushes into flour instead of cracking cleanly and loses extract. Warm, damp storage also invites weevils and mould.

Keep malt in sealed bags or a closed silo, off the floor and away from walls. Use stock in the order it arrived. Check moisture on older lots before milling. A cheap moisture meter pays for itself the first time it stops you milling a damp lot.

• Agree a specification with your maltster and get a certificate of analysis per lot.
  • Measure your own spirit yield per tonne and track it by lot.
  • Sieve test the grist every shift and adjust the mill gap with the lot.
  • Check conversion with iodine and log first wort gravity.
  • Control washback peak temperature and leave room for foam.
  • Taste the new make by lot so you can link flavour back to the barley.

Done consistently, these turn local barley from a risk into a known, costed ingredient.
faqs: Can you make good single malt from six-row barley?
Yes. Several Indian single malts use Indian six-row barley. It needs adjusted milling and mashing and gives a lower yield per tonne than premium two-row malt.
Why does six-row barley have higher enzyme power?
It usually has more protein. Enzymes are proteins. After malting that shows up as higher diastatic power, which helps starch conversion.
Does six-row barley give a different flavour?
Often a little more grainy and husky. Fermentation, distillation and the cask still shape most of the final flavour.
